The Apostle *Paul* warns
his son *Timothy* that he
should *reject the questions* that
are *foolish and without instruction, know-*
*ing that they bring forth strife*, <note>A reference to 2 Timothy 2:23: "But foolish and unlearned questions avoid, knowing that they do gender strifes."</note>

*godliness* <note>original Dutch: "Godtloofheidt," referring to 2 Timothy 2:16</note>. These are also presently those days in which people have a great desire to present many controversial questions to one another, and to handle them with great vehemence and shouting. Yet, when one considers it well, it is found that it indeed follows the word of the Apostle, *that they increase unto more ungodliness*. I have also allowed myself to be drawn a bit too far into those vain and foolish questions, but as I have since noticed, and am now forced to my shame to confess—

<meta>This page continues the dedication by Jacobus Koelman to Daniel Beukelaar and Catharina Brugmans. Koelman is reflecting on his own past involvement in theological disputes and explaining his pivot toward the "practical godliness" found in English Puritan literature.</meta>

—to confess, to the detriment and decrease of godliness, and to the increase and growth in ungodliness. Oh, that others would learn from my example to be more cautious: Now I thank God that He has enlightened my eyes and drawn my desire away from that foolish wisdom; He has prepared a better wisdom for His children, which powerfully brings them out of darkness into the light, and causes them to grow in the fear of God and holiness.

One must admit that in *England* the Church of Christ has flourished most of all during the past sixty or seventy years; and from where else has this come than because the practice and the power of godliness <term>Godtzaligheid: a core concept of the Dutch "Nadere Reformatie" (Further Reformation), emphasizing that true faith must be expressed through a life of active, inner piety</term> were more esteemed among the people there than many contentious questions, and because the teachers insisted upon it with all zeal, both in their public sermons and in their writings; so that people now mostly derive that powerful way of teaching from them. I have also, to that end, made myself somewhat familiar with that language <note>Referring to the English language, which Koelman learned specifically to access Puritan devotional works</note>; and among others, the work of this author *Christopher Love* <note>Christopher Love (1618–1651) was a popular English Presbyterian minister whose works were widely translated into Dutch due to their focus on the "anatomy" of the soul and Christian struggle</note> came into my hands, in which I took a particular pleasure,

# DEDICATION.

because I saw that he not only solemnly resolved many difficult cases of conscience <term>Gevallen van Conscientie: "Cases of conscience" refers to casuistry, the practice of resolving specific moral dilemmas or spiritual doubts by applying religious principles</term>, but also that he vividly depicted the specific obstacles in the way of godliness <term>Godtzaligheid: a life of active, heartfelt piety and devotion to God</term>, as if from his own experience, and powerfully armed man against them. Especially, I think, he has shown that in this treatise, *The Struggle between Flesh and Spirit, etc.* <note>original: "Van den Strijdt tusschen Vleesch en Geest, &c."</note>, which I—because I felt that it very nakedly revealed my own miserable state to me and prescribed remedies against it—have therefore, alongside my private occupations, translated into our language, so that it might also serve for the edification of many others. And although I could not pay much attention to the elegance of the words, I nevertheless know that the author’s meaning will clearly appear even to the unlearned. The Author (which is remarkable) only permitted this little book to be made public through print; for he had a greater affection for it than for any of his other works, as he himself testified to two ministers <term>Predikanten: ordained clergy in the Reformed tradition</term>, a few days before his death <note>Christopher Love was executed by beheading in 1651 for his involvement in a plot to restore the monarchy; his "last words" and final works were highly prized by his followers</note>; and truly the blessed outcome of his Spir-

Now, I have wished to dedicate this little book <term>Boekjen: a common 17th-century term for a devotional treatise or "booklet"</term> to you, partly to give a public sign of my grateful acknowledgment of the special and uncommon friendship you have shown me; and partly because I hope, indeed firmly trust, that the subject matter itself will be most pleasing to you, and that it will refresh your souls more than the flowing honey did for *Jonathan* <note>A reference to 1 Samuel 14:27, where Jonathan’s eyes were brightened after eating wild honey during a battle; here used as a metaphor for spiritual enlightenment and strength</note>; as I also noticed to some extent when we recently spoke together about the sorrowful withdrawal of God’s Spirit, and of the Struggle that exists within believers between the Spirit and the Flesh.

This little book will provide you with specific guidance on how lamentable and utterly miserable it is when God’s Spirit withdraws His cooperation and influences from our religious exercises <term>Godts-dienst-plegingen: acts of worship or religious duties</term>, and consequently how carefully all professors <term>Belijders: those who publicly profess their faith; synonymous with "believers" or "confessors" in this period</term> must then guard themselves against *grieving or quenching the Spirit*...

Here it is also shown how precious and powerful the influence of the Holy Spirit is when it pleases Him, through His gracious indwelling <term>by-wooninghe: the theological concept of the Spirit living within the believer</term>, to make our religious services powerful, so that we must rightly pray with the Bride <note>The "Bride" refers to the Church or the individual soul as described in the Song of Solomon</note>; *Awake, O north wind; and come, thou south; blow upon my garden, that the spices thereof may flow out: O that my beloved might come to his garden and eat his pleasant fruits!* <note>original: "Ontwaakt Noorden-windt, ende komt ghy Zuyden-windt, doorwaeye mijnen Hof, dat fijne Speceryen uit-vloeyen: O dat mijn lieffste tot mijnen Hof quame ende ate fijne edele vrughten!" — a translation of Song of Solomon 4:16</note> You will also find here comforting aids and rules for walking by the Spirit and following His guidance, who is mighty *to lead you into all truth.* Lastly, you will see described here very emphatically that direct conflict that exists between Flesh and Spirit: since in the heart of every Christian (just as in the womb of *Rebekah*) there are two conflicting things, struggling against each other <note>A reference to Genesis 25:22-23, where the struggling twins Jacob and Esau represent the internal conflict between a person's sinful nature and their spiritual nature</note>. But this is our comfort: *The elder shall serve the younger*; corruption will, like the house of *Saul*, decrease step by step, and grace will, like the house of *David*, grow and become stronger and stronger throughout <note>Referring to 2 Samuel 3:1, where the decline of Saul’s house and the rise of David’s house serve as a metaphor for the gradual victory of God's grace over human sin</note>. # DEDICATION.

and [I] hope that you will also be furthered by this in the way of godliness <term>Godtzaligheit: a central concept in the Dutch Second Reformation referring to a life lived in practical, heartfelt devotion to God</term>, and more *built up in your most holy faith.* In closing, I pray to our God from the bottom of my heart for you both, that He may let you live together happily for many days, *walking in the fear of the Lord* and *the comfort of the Holy Spirit, and that His truth may be a buckler and a shield to you* <note>original: "rondasse ende Beukelaar" — both terms refer to types of shields; this is a reference to Psalm 91:4</note>. # To the Nazirites of the Lord.
<note>original: "Nazireërs" — Referring to the biblical Nazirites (Numbers 6) who were "set apart" by a vow for God's service. The author uses this as a title for ministers and theological students who are dedicated to holy work.</note>

...find, that it must first be taken in hand by the Ministers of the Word themselves, who must not only with all earnestness and zeal observe this most necessary, profitable, and glorious work in others, as this also applies to them, yes, especially and before all others:
<margin>* See Mr. Willem Teellinck <note>Willem Teellinck (1579–1629) was the father of the Dutch *Nadere Reformatie*, a movement similar to English Puritanism that emphasized personal piety.</note>, *Necessary Discourse* <note>original: "Nootwendigh Vertoogh"</note>, Book 1, Chapters 10 & 11.</margin>
* but they must begin with themselves, if they wish to perform good work: for from them, without doubt, the decay and lukewarmness among Christians first sprang forth; through their lack of zeal, the zeal of the people has declined; through their misconduct, the Congregation has fallen, because the Sheep follow the Shepherd. One still sees (and how pitiful and lamentable this is!) that so many hirelings <note>original: "huurlingen" — a biblical reference (John 10:12) to ministers who serve for money or status rather than for the spiritual care of their flock.</note> have crept into our Churches; who have no good purpose in their service, among whom that zeal, that practice of godliness <term>Godzaligheit: a central concept in the Dutch Second Reformation, referring to an active, heartfelt devotion to God that manifests in all areas of life</term>, that excellent holiness which was in our first Reformers, is not to be found. But my intention is not to point out their faults, and to set their guilty duty before their eyes.
<margin>† W. Teellinck, *Warning of Zephaniah* <note>original: "waarschouwinge Zephaniæ"</note> Chapter 5. *Necessary Discourse*, Book 6, Chapter 3. Godefridus Udemans <note>A prominent Dutch minister known for his works on ethics and trade.</note>, *Heavenly Siege* <note>original: "Hemels belegh"</note> on Matthew 11, verse 12, the 7th Doctrine, page 113 and following.</margin>
† Other renowned zealots and heroes of God have done that; it would also not be proper for me: I only wish to slightly awaken myself and my fellow brothers, who are training at the Universities <term>Hooge-schoolen: literally "High Schools," referring to the universities of the time (like Leiden or Utrecht) where theology was studied</term> and preparing themselves for the service of the Word.

The Universities (it is true) are nurseries <note>original: "Plant-hoven" — literally "plant-gardens" or orchards, a common metaphor for universities as places where future leaders are grown.</note>, from which the leaders in the Church and the State <note>original: "Politie" — refers to civil governance and the social order, not the modern police force.</note> must come; and yet it is seen daily, that among the students of Holy Divinity <note>original: "Godt-geleertheit" — Theology.</note> (to speak only of that now) the practice of...

# A Christian Address

true godliness <term>Godzaligheit: a central concept in the Dutch Second Reformation, referring to an active, heartfelt devotion to God that manifests in all areas of life</term> is so seldom practiced, and the power of it so little felt, that it cannot be sufficiently lamented. There are very striking words from that faithful servant **Mr. Love** <note>Christopher Love (1618–1651) was a prominent Presbyterian minister in England executed for his involvement in a plot to restore Charles II. His "speech on the scaffold" was widely circulated among Reformed Christians as a model of martyrdom.</note>, in his last speech on the **Scaffold**, which I have read with rejoicing and emotion in my heart: *Praise be to God*, he said, *who has not 
,, only made me a Christian, but also a 
,, Preacher: and He, finding that I 
,, would be faithful, has entrusted the Ministry to me; 
,, it is an honor to me that I die thus; I would rather be a Pre-
,, acher in a Pulpit, than a King on a 
,, Throne; I would rather be an instrument to 
,, bring souls to Heaven, than that all Nations should 
,, pay me toll and tribute; let men judge of me 
,, what they will, I am nonetheless a Martyr, etc.* 

Truly, it is a very great honor for us—who are poor **earth-worms** and foul, worthless **fiends of hell** <note>original: *helle-wichten*. A term of extreme self-abasement common in 17th-century pietism to emphasize God's grace.</note>, just like others—that we are chosen out of thousands to be sent as **Ambassadors** of the living God, to become **Caretakers of Souls** and **Watchmen** over the sheep of the Chief Shepherd; to restore the image of Almighty God within man according to our measure; and to be, in a special manner, the servants of the Lord. The servants of **Solomon** were considered happy because they could always stand before the face of that wise King, but here is one greater than Solomon, who calls us to Him on the mountain in His **Cabinet** <note>A private room for study or counsel.</note>, and allows us to understand and feel many fine secrets much more closely than others. He desires that we shall step into the breaches and wall up the wall for the house of **Israel**, to stand in the battle in the day of the Lord, and to be the **chariots and horsemen of Israel** <note>A biblical reference to 2 Kings 2:12, suggesting that godly leaders are the true defense of a nation.</note>. Yes, He who hereafter shall let us shine like the brightness of the firmament, and like the stars forever and ever. 

Concluding with this, I pray to the Lord **Jesus Christ**, our crucified **Savior**, that He—to me, who am the least and unworthiest of all, and to all of you together—will so prepare and enable us that we, through teaching and life, may win many and bring them to Christ. Amen.

This chapter contains within itself two parts; first, God’s intention to cause the world to perish by the flood <note>original: *water-vloet*</note>. Second, God’s providence <note>original: *voor-ſorghe*</note> in preserving Noah and his entire household in this general judgment, through the preparation of an Ark.

Our text falls under the first main section, namely under the intention to destroy the world by a flood. Concerning this judgment, the burgeoning <note>original: *voort-telende*. This is why the Lord God intended to destroy the world.

# The Withdrawal

...service; yet his days shall be a hundred and twenty years; that is, another hundred and twenty years shall pass by before the flood shall come over them.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
But here now lies an objection: how can it be said that there would be a hundred and twenty years before the flood would come when these words were spoken, since at that time Noah was five hundred years old, and the flood came when he was six hundred years old? <note>According to Genesis 5:32 and 7:6, there is a 100-year gap between Noah fathering his sons and the start of the Flood, creating a conflict with the 120-year period mentioned in Genesis 6:3.</note> Would there then be twenty years less than God had promised?

This is a very tangled knot, and the interpreters go to great effort to untie it and to defend God's faithfulness in this: let God be true, and every man a liar. <note>A reference to Romans 3:4: "Let God be true, and every human being a liar."</note> <margin>Jerome</margin> <term>Jerome<gloss>Known as Hieronymus in the original text; a 4th-century Church Father best known for translating the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</gloss></term> answers that God indeed promised a hundred and twenty years, but that the wickedness of mankind between the making of that promise and its fulfillment grew so much, and provoked God to such anger, that He withdrew twenty years from the promise. <margin>Musculus</margin> So also says <term>Musculus<gloss>Wolfgang Musculus (1497–1563), an influential German Protestant theologian and biblical commentator.</gloss></term>, who adds to this that God, in making a promise, retains the condition within Himself: for just as God can refrain from bringing a judgment which He threatens against a people if they quickly repent—as we have an example of this in the <term>Ninevites<gloss>The people of Nineveh who, in the Book of Jonah, repented and were subsequently spared from the destruction God had threatened.</gloss></term>—so He is also not bound to [grant] them the promised...

...to give harm in the event of willful, stubborn, and incorrigible wickedness, just as we see in the household of Eli. <margin>Answer.</margin>
But the best and correct answer to this is this: namely, that this promise <note>The "promise" here refers to the 120-year period of grace granted before the Flood.</note> was not made to Noah when he was five hundred years old, but when he was four hundred and eighty years old. For although it was said in the fifth chapter at the final verse that Noah was five hundred years old, it is nonetheless not said there that he was that old when this promise was made. This is the interpretation of <term>Rivetus<gloss>Andreas Rivetus (1572–1651), a highly influential French Huguenot theologian who taught in Leiden.</gloss></term>, <term>Mercerus<gloss>Jean Mercier (c. 1510–1570), a famous French Hebraist and scholar of the Hebrew Bible.</gloss></term>, and others.

<margin>Objection.</margin>

## Of God’s Spirit.

...pay attention to these following six warnings and propositions.

<margin>1st Proposition.</margin>
Ensure that you are certain / that you do not err by mistaking moral persuasions <term>moral persuasions: an intellectual or emotional conviction reached through human reasoning or powerful preaching, which mimics true conversion but lacks a supernatural change of heart.</term> for a special working of the Spirit within you. Whenever human reason is convinced by the strong proofs of Scripture / then there is a moral persuasion / and in this way the Word of God can bring a person quite far / and yet it is only a common working <term>common working: a general influence of the Spirit that affects the mind or emotions of many, including those who may not ultimately be saved.</term> of the Spirit. # ### About God's Spirit.

God withdrew his Spirit so that it would not strive with the people of the ancient world <note>The "old world" refers to the era of humanity before the Great Flood.</note>; it was their disobedience, <margin>1 Peter 3:19, 20.</margin> as the Apostle *Peter* speaks: *Christ* went by his Spirit and preached to the spirits who are in prison, who formerly were disobedient, when the longsuffering of God once waited in the days of *Noah* <note>original: "Noë"</note>. Their disobedience caused God to withdraw the power of his spirit. If, then, the Spirit does not work upon you, do not think ill of God, but blame yourself; he is provoked to this. Likewise, God withdrew from the people of *Israel* because of their sins. <margin>Psalm 81:12, 13.</margin> "But my people did not hear my voice, and *Israel* did not want me. Therefore I gave them over to the stubbornness <note>original: "goet-dunken," literally meaning one's own opinion or whim.</note> of their hearts, so that they walked in their own counsels."

The Spirit is compared in the Scripture to a Dove. Now, a dove will always stay in the house where it was raised, unless the dovecote <note>original: "Duyven-huys."</note>, being full of stench, is not cleaned. The Spirit of God can aptly be compared to a dove in this regard; keep your hearts pure, and the Spirit will remain with you; but keep them stinking, and the spirit will soon leave you. Sin is therefore the cause why the Spirit withdraws from the established means of worship <note>term: *in-gestelde middelen van Godts-dienst*. The "means of grace," such as preaching and sacraments, through which God was believed to interact with believers.</note>, and people are left to themselves; and God does this as an act of his justice, punishing sin.

Perhaps you have sinned unknowingly, suddenly, vehemently, and with premeditation: certainly, the more the **Spirit** was withheld from you before the sin, pray that He may contend with you all the more afterward, and that in these three ways:

1. That He may work in you a clearer conviction of sin; that He may show it to you, not in general terms, but in particular, clothed with all its shameful and aggravating circumstances, to convict you for your salvation <term>zaligheid<gloss>the state of being saved or eternal blessedness</gloss></term>, so that a kind of recompense <note>The author suggests a spiritual "balance"; if the Spirit was silent before the sin, His voice must be twice as loud in the repentance following it.</note> may occur for the fact that the **Spirit** was previously withheld from you.

2. That He may humble you more deeply. According to how much the **Spirit** was withheld from you before the sin, desire that He may cast you down all the more after the sinning. This was prefigured <note>In 17th-century theology, Old Testament laws were often interpreted as "types" or "figures" that illustrated spiritual realities of the soul.</note> under the Law: he who merely touched an unclean thing was unclean until the evening, but he who had carried something unclean with him had to cast off all his clothes. So also, if you have only touched a sin, you must humble yourself; but if you have fallen into a sin of which the **Spirit** did not convict you beforehand, then you must strive for a greater measure of conviction and humiliation afterward.

# Concerning the Spirit of God

...nor should we let our devotion cause us to neglect our duty toward fellow man. You have a notable text regarding this in the Gospel of Matthew. The Scribes and Pharisees had taught this doctrine: that if any person had voluntarily and generously given toward godly uses, he was then free from those duties which he owed to his father and mother. <margin>Galatians 5, verse 4, compared with verse 8.</margin>

### Of God’s Spirit

...en someone who is close to you is in a dangerous illness, and you, out of love for God's Word, want to go and hear the same, and thus neglect your sick friend; in this case, God the Lord would rather that you show mercy than sacrifice <note>original: "barmhertigheit doet dan offerhande"; a reference to the biblical principle in Matthew 9:13 and Hosea 6:6, emphasizing that practical compassion for others is more pleasing to God than religious rituals.</note>. Everything is most beautiful in its own time <note>A reference to Ecclesiastes 3:11.</note>. 

Again, suppose that servants, when they are engaged in their masters’ work—and the welfare of their masters depends on their diligence—receive an impulse to pray, or to hear God’s word, and thus to perform religious duties whereby the work of the masters is neglected; then this is a sin and comes from the Devil. The reason is this: because God regards the servants and their time as not being their own <note>In the 17th-century context, a servant's labor and time were legally contracted to the employer; using that time for personal prayer was considered a violation of that contract and a "theft" of time.</note>. Therefore, they shall please God more at that time by doing their masters’ work than if they lay on their knees and prayed. 

Now, I do not relate this to make anyone harsh toward their servants, but rather to encourage masters to grant them more time for their souls and to serve God. Nor do I wish to extinguish any good impulses toward goodness that are in them, as some evil and worldly masters do to their godly servants. But this I would advise the servants: that they should take no time from their necessary work for holy duties whereby their masters might be harmed, but rather take it from their sleep, and use those idle hours for prayer which are granted to them.

# The Withdrawal

<margin>Use for consolation.</margin>

So that no troubled conscience might in any way be discouraged by what I have said / I shall propose four words of consolation for such people.

<margin>I.</margin>

Firstly, consider / that although the life-giving workings of the Spirit may be withdrawn from a godly person / nevertheless the gracious presence of the Spirit cannot be withdrawn. <margin>Question 3.</margin> But what kind of benefit will result from this? You shall not fulfill the <term>lust of the flesh</term> <note>A common biblical phrase (from Galatians 5:16) referring to the desires of the fallen human nature.</note>.

<margin>Answer.</margin> Before I come to answer this, I must warn you of this: namely, that the Apostle does not say that you will then not *have* the lust of the flesh. For, as you know, he who most follows the movements and directions of the Spirit in his practice also finds within himself the workings of corrupt nature. As long as you have this natural body, you will also have within you this lust of the flesh; but the Apostle says, "You shall not **fulfill** the lust of the flesh." <margin>3. Question.</margin>
But what benefit will arise from this? *You shall not fulfill the lust of the flesh.*

<margin>Answer.</margin>
Before I come to answer this, I must warn you of this: namely, that the Apostle does not say, you shall then not *have* the lust of the flesh. For, as you know, even he who most diligently follows the movements and guidances of the Spirit in his spiritual practice also finds within himself the workings of a corrupt nature. As long as you have this natural body, you will also have this lust of the flesh within you; but the Apostle says, *You shall not fulfill the lust of the flesh.* 

Now, by "the lusts of the flesh," you must not understand it in a narrow sense as the sin of sensuality or impurity (which in other places is rightly also called the lust of the flesh); rather, you must take it in a broad and general sense, for all those corrupt and disordered inclinations toward sin which exist in the nature of man. When the Apostle then says, "you shall not fulfill these lusts," the meaning is not that you shall not sin, but that you shall not commit sin with such strong and full consent, nor with such intent as unregenerate <term>unregenerate: those who have not undergone a spiritual rebirth or conversion</term> people, who do not have God's Spirit.

# By the Spirit.

...fill [them] <note>completing the sentence from the previous page: "how can this be true, that if we walk by the Spirit, we shall not fulfill the lust of the flesh?"</note>, even though experience teaches us that however precisely and carefully a person walks, and however spiritual they may be, they will nevertheless incline toward the desires of the flesh and practice them; and that corruption which lies hidden in their nature will break out in their life!

<margin>Answer.</margin>
I have two things to answer to this:

First, although a person walking by the Spirit will truly have the desires of the flesh, it is nonetheless no less true that a godly person walking in this way will not *fulfill* the desire of the flesh; the reason is this. There is a distinction between the *working* and the *fulfilling* of the desires of the flesh. When a godly person sins, he indeed "works" <note>The author uses "werken" (working/operating) to describe the involuntary or resisted presence of sin, as opposed to its completion.</note> the desire of the flesh, but he does not *fulfill* it, because he does not then commit the sin with such full consent, nor with such deliberate and complete operation of his will as the ungodly do. Sin carries away the ungodly with greater violence and power, and with a more premeditated action of the will. This is how some interpreters resolve this difficulty.

<margin>Musculus <note>Wolfgang Musculus (1497–1563) was an influential Protestant reformer and theologian whose biblical commentaries were standard academic texts in the 17th century.</note> on this passage.</margin>

<margin>1. Question.</margin>
Why must a believer walk according to the guidance of God’s Spirit? And what are the reasons for this?

<margin>1. Reason.</margin>
1. Because it is a significant part of the **office of the Spirit** <note>original: "ampt des Geests"; in 17th-century theology, an "office" refers to a specific duty or role assigned to a person of the Trinity</note>—following the grace of conversion—to awaken the heart and to move it toward greater grace, and to lead the person on the path upon which he must walk. This was expressed in this way by the Prophet Isaiah: *And your ears shall hear* <margin>Isaiah 30:21</margin> *the word of the one who is behind you, saying, "this is the way, walk in it," whenever you would turn aside to the right or to the left hand.* <margin>Matthew 2:9</margin> What the **Star** was for the **Wise Men from the East**, and the **pillar of fire** for the people of Israel as they journeyed through the **Wilderness**: that is also what the Spirit is for the Believer, in leading them upon the eternal way. If you then do not walk according to the movements and the guidance of the Spirit, you hinder the office of the Spirit as much as is within you.

<margin>2. Reason.</margin>
2. Therefore, it is your bounden duty to walk according to the guidance of God’s Spirit because the **Devil** always seeks to suggest evil things to you; he roams about <margin>Job 1:7</margin> upon the earth and walks through it, not to do good but to do evil; he goes about seeking whom he might devour. <margin>1 Peter 5:8</margin> And not only the Devil, but also your **own spirit** <note>The author distinguishes here between the Holy Spirit and the human "spirit" or fallen nature</note> is a false spirit, enticing you and stirring you toward sin: just as a **glowing oven** <note>original: "gloependen Oven"; a vivid metaphor for a white-hot or blazing furnace</note> casts out sparks, and the chimney casts out smoke, so your own spirit gives out sinful impulses.

There is no profit in following the flesh, but indeed in walking in the Spirit. Luther <note>Martin Luther (1483–1546), the German Reformer. His commentaries were foundational for the Dutch Reformed tradition from which this text likely stems.</note> has an apt explanation regarding what Paul says,
<margin>Romans 13:12.</margin>
> Let us cast off the works of darkness, and put on the armor of light.

Sin is called a work of darkness, and if one wants to pay attention to the contrast, grace should have been called a "work of light"; but it is not named so, but rather the "armor of light" <note>Original: *wapenen des lichts*. While *wapenen* can mean weapons, in the context of Paul’s "armor of God," it refers to defensive and offensive gear.</note>. Why is such an unequal contrast made here? Luther gives this reason: sin is called a "work" of darkness, and not "armor," to make known that there is no power in it against the wrath of God; but grace is called the "armor" of light because, just as armor is for adornment and protection, so too grace adorns the soul and preserves it from the coming wrath. <margin>Romans 8:6.</margin>
> the minding of the flesh is death, but the minding of the Spirit is life and peace.

<margin>1. Question.</margin>
What is meant by those words, *the lusts of the flesh*?

<margin>1. Answer.</margin>
If one takes the natural desires of the body to be the "lusts of the flesh," then the truth of this text cannot hold: for we may indeed fulfill the natural appetite and longing of the body, as we do when we feed it when it is hungry, give it drink when it is thirsty, and give it rest when it is weary. Thus, one may lawfully fulfill the lusts of the flesh if they are understood as the natural desires of the body; therefore, it cannot be understood in that way here.

<margin>II.</margin>
2. Furthermore, it must not be limited to the sin of unbridled wantonness <note>original: "wulpsheit," usually referring to sexual immorality or excessive indulgence</note>, but it must be taken in a broad and comprehensive sense for the sinfulness of our **corrupt nature**, whose desires and movements one must not fulfill.

<margin>III. The first and second act <note>original: "Actus primus & secundus," Scholastic terms used to distinguish between a capacity and its actual use</note>.</margin>

# By the Spirit.

...not fulfill. This is what the English Translation follows, but it also places (as can be seen) the alternative translation and reading in the margin. However, it is of little consequence which way it is taken. <note>The author refers to the interpretive choice between seeing this as a direct command or a promised result of walking by the Spirit.</note>

<margin>II.</margin>
Secondly, this promise should not be taken absolutely or unconditionally (as it may appear), but conditionally. By this I mean: God does not promise this absolutely, but on this condition: *If you walk by the Spirit*, then, on this condition, you shall not fulfill the lusts of the flesh.

<margin>III.</margin>
Thirdly, it does not say: you shall not *have* the lusts of the flesh; for who lives on earth who does not have them? Rather: you shall not *fulfill* them.

<margin>IV.</margin>
Fourthly, in the English translation one reads "the lusts of the flesh" <note>plural</note>; but in the Greek it says "the lust of the flesh" in the singular.
<margin><note>original Greek: ἐπιθυμίαν σαρκός (*epithymian sarkos*), meaning "lust of the flesh"</note></margin>
What might be the reason that the word, being in the singular in the original text, is read there in the plural? The reason is this: because, although the <term>sin of nature: "zonde der natuur," the inherent corruption or original sin present in all humans</term> is but a single "lump" of sin (so to speak), it nonetheless contains many sins within itself. From this translation, we can draw this application: that although the sin of nature is but one, all the sins of the world are nevertheless contained within it, as in a seed.

# On Walking [by the Spirit]

<margin>V.</margin>
Fifthly, regarding the associated result: there is no reason why any doubt should be left in your hearts that this benefit will not be granted to you, provided you fulfill the conditions. Walk by the Spirit, and God will preserve you, so that you will not fulfill the <term>desires of the flesh: "begeerlijkheden des vleesches," referring to the worldly or sinful impulses of human nature</term>. I derive this from the Apostle’s <note>The "Apostle" refers to Paul, specifically in Galatians 5:16.</note> affirmation in these words: *And I say, walk by the Spirit, and you shall not fulfill the desires of the flesh.* "And I say" is as if the Apostle said: "This is what I have to speak to you in the name of the Lord—that if you walk by the Spirit, you shall not fulfill [these desires]," etc. These specific points having been set forth, here is the Doctrine.

<margin>Doctrine.</margin>
That walking according to the guidance and movements of the Spirit is a particular means for a person, so that they shall not carry out the desires of the flesh with such a strong and full impulse of the will as wicked and ungodly people do when they sin against God.

In the treatment of this matter, I shall lay open this one thing alone: namely, how the ungodly commit sins and fulfill the desires of the flesh, and in what manner the godly—who walk according to the guidance of the Spirit—shall not sin.

<margin>1. Distinction.</margin>
Firstly, those who walk according to the Spirit shall not sin as willfully or as intentionally as the ungodly. *For* <margin>Heb. 10 v. 26.</margin> *if we sin willfully after we have received the knowledge of the truth, there remains no more sacrifice for sins.* The godly do not sin with such a strong impulse of the will as the ungodly do. They do indeed sin, and also with their will, but there is in the will much resistance against the will; there is no full consent of the will, nor any full impulse and striving of the heart. Therefore, <margin>Rom. 7 v. 19.</margin> the Apostle *Paul* says, *the evil that I do not want, that I do.* *Paul* says indeed that he did the evil; but he also says that he did not want the evil that he did. A believing person sometimes surrenders themselves to sin as to a powerful <term>tyrant: "dwingle-landt," literally a 'forcing-land,' used here to mean an oppressive or illegitimate ruler who usurps power</term>, but not as to their natural Lord. Wicked people want the evil that they do, but the pious want the good that they do not do. This manner of speaking is taken from the blacksmiths, who, whenever they wish to bring a piece of iron to a neat shape or form, lay it in the forge. The ungodly are as skillful and cunning in the way of sin as if they had been trained in a school for it. Therefore we read of them that their tongues are said to "couple deceit." <note>The original Dutch *koppelen* suggests yoking or linking things together with intent.</note> It is written that Christ, on the last day, shall reject those who are "workers of iniquity." All men indeed commit iniquity, but not all "work" iniquity; that is, they do not make a <term>trade: an "Ambacht" or professional craft</term> of sinning, nor are they skillful in the cursed art of sinning.

<margin>
6. Distinction.
</margin>
**Sixthly**, the godly do not sin with such premeditation and intent as the ungodly do. It is true, a pious man can be brought to sin through the powerful violence of temptation and through the treachery of his own heart, but he does not deliberate over the sin, nor does he go about quietly considering within himself how he might commit the sin.

The conflict between flesh [and Spirit]

## Galatians 5:17.

->For the flesh desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh, and these stand against one another, so that you do not do that which you would.<-

<margin>
12th Sermon in St. Lawrence Jewry <note>original: "Laurence Jurii"; referring to the historic church of St. Lawrence Jewry in the City of London, where many influential Puritan-leaning sermons were held in the 17th century.</note> within London, the 15th of December, 1650.
</margin>

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut drop cap 'N' decorated with floral scrolls and vines.</image-desc>

After I have dealt with the preceding verse in several sermons regarding walking by the Spirit; I now proceed to the treatment of this verse, which contains within itself the conflict between the flesh and the Spirit.

At this time I shall only explain the first small part of the text, and after that I shall deal with the others in their proper order.

The first attack in this spiritual case occurs through the flesh; the flesh desires against the Spirit.

To open this up, I shall explain two things:
1. What is understood by "the flesh"?
2. What is meant by "the Spirit"? And then, what is meant by the desiring of the flesh against the Spirit?

<margin>
1st Question answered.
</margin>

By the flesh, the corruption of human nature caused by original sin <term>original sin: the theological concept that all humans are born with a secondary, sinful nature inherited from the Fall of Man</term> must be understood. This corruption can be viewed either as a habit <term>habit: from the Dutch 'heblijkheit,' meaning an internal disposition or a settled state of being, rather than a single act</term> or as an operation <term>operation: from 'werkinge,' referring to the active manifestation or outworking of that sinful nature</term>. If one views the flesh as a habit, then it points to that first root and original disorder <term>disorder: 'wanschiklijkheid,' implying a lack of proper spiritual arrangement or a deformity of the soul</term> in

The author begins by defining "the flesh" as the inherited corruption of human nature that exists both as an internal disposition and through its active operations.</summary>

### and S P I R I T.

in man’s nature toward the good. But if it is taken as an **action**, then it signifies our **corrupted movements** against grace; and so I take it in this place: *the flesh desires against the Spirit*; that is, when the Spirit of God, through Divine knockings, strikes the heart with holy movements, then there is a conflict of the flesh against these movements, by suppressing them and bringing the heart to evil.

The corruption of nature may be called **flesh** for these reasons:

<margin>I.</margin> Firstly, because the soul was infected with corruption immediately following its union and joining with the body. It is true, there is a dispute among theologians <note>original: "Godt-geleerden"</note> regarding when the soul becomes corrupted, since it is infused through creation <note>This refers to the theological doctrine of "Creationism" (distinct from the modern term), which posits that God creates a new, pure soul for every human body at conception. This created a debate: if the soul is created pure by God, how does it become "corrupted" by original sin?</note> and is therefore pure! But almost all authors agree on this: that immediately upon the union of the soul with the body, man is said to have natural corruption; and for this reason, some believe that the corrupted nature is called **flesh**, because man is naturally corrupted as soon as soul and body are coupled together.

...works against the Spirit: although sin is of an active nature, it is nevertheless not always working, but indeed always desiring; there is an opposing disposition and form in the nature against the work of God’s Spirit upon the heart. In these words, one must take note of three parts:

<margin>Doctrine.</margin>

I shall not dwell long on proving this point; it stands clearly in God’s Word, and every person has experience of it; therefore, in treating this, I shall answer several questions, and after that, I shall provide you with the practical application <note>original: "nuttigheit," literally "utility" or "usefulness," a standard part of a sermon focusing on how the listener should apply the lesson</note>.

# THE CONFLICT BETWEEN FLESH

<margin>IV. Blessed is he alone whose reward is faithful <note>original: "zalighen is het alleen/wiens loon trouw is"</note>.</margin>

Fourthly, by persuading you to maintain **small sins** <note>original: "kleine zonden"</note>, with the promise that if you only indulge in these, you will never come to commit the greater ones. This is a great deceitfulness of the heart, through which thousands have fallen; for small sins are nevertheless an entrance to greater sins. A small thief placed inside a house can open the doors so that larger and stronger thieves may enter. 

I have read a story of a **young man** <note>original: "Jonghelingh"</note> who was tempted by the **Devil** <note>original: "Duyvel"</note> and his own heart to commit three sins: namely, to murder his **father**, to dishonor his **mother**, and to get drunk. He did not wish to do the first two sins, as he naturally had a horror of them; but he thought, "I will give myself to the last one," because that sin was the smallest—which was nevertheless enough to cause the others: for while being drunk, he killed his father and dishonored his own mother. 

Guard yourself then against this deceit of sin. Your heart will not at first advise you to commit all sins; but will seek to draw you there by degrees, from smaller to greater sins, until you become abominable in them. See (says the Apostle <margin>James 3:5</margin> James), how great a pile of wood a small fire sets ablaze! Small, permitted sins may be the opportunity to bring forth many great sins. Therefore, beware that you are not deceived.

and SPIRIT.

<margin>The first sin was every sin. <note>original Latin: "Primum peccatum fuit omne peccatum."</note></margin>
**through the commandment; has in me (says the Apostle)** <note>A reference to the Apostle Paul in Romans 7:8: "But sin, taking occasion by the commandment, wrought in me all manner of concupiscence."</note> **wrought all desire.** Corrupt nature is an inclination toward all actual evil in the world. This can be explained through the example of an egg. An egg contains within itself, in potential and in its seed, all the parts of a chicken; it only lacks the warmth of the hen to brood and bring it forth. In the same way, our corrupt flesh contains all sin within itself, and just as the hen brings forth the chick, so too does the Devil brood upon sin.

3. It sets itself against all the graces of God's Spirit; take whatever other sin you will, these only stand against a specific, contrary grace. Particular sins have only a particular opposition; for example: the sin of pride sets itself against humility, greed against mercy, drunkenness against sobriety, injustice against righteousness, anger against gentleness, hate against love, and so with all other sins. They have only a particular opposition to particular gifts of grace, but your flesh sets itself generally against all grace.

<margin>4. Quality.</margin>

208 The Struggle Between the Flesh

corrupt nature is like those four things <margin>Proverbs 30:16</margin> of which Solomon says they are never satisfied <note>Proverbs 30:15–16 mentions the grave, the barren womb, the parched earth, and fire as four things that never say "Enough."</note>; and as he speaks elsewhere <margin>Proverbs 27:20</margin>, **Hell and destruction are never satisfied; so the eyes of man are not satisfied,** that is, the corrupt nature acting through the eye. Sinful desire in the heart ensures that an adulterous eye is never satisfied.

2. In respect to both punishment and sin. Suppose that sin brings diseases upon your body, or poverty upon your estate, yet you would still not abandon sin; the flesh even loves the damnation of your soul.

<margin>5. Quality.</margin>
Fifthly, the flesh is an untiring enemy against the Spirit. Suppose the flesh possessed all the previously mentioned characteristics, but lacked this one; then there would still be hope that it would eventually become weary and exhausted. But this is the inherent nature of corruption: it is hostile toward the Spirit without ever growing tired. Things that act by their very nature do not grow weary of acting; fire is never tired of burning, nor the water of ebbing and flowing, because those actions are natural to those creatures. The Sun is never weary of running its course, because that movement is natural to it. Sin is natural to you—it is the state in which you were born and raised—and therefore it works without becoming tired. This war between flesh and Spirit is without any ceasefire.

<margin>7. Quality.</margin> Seventhly, this corruption of nature is a constant enemy against the Spirit. There is nothing which works without ceasing except for this corrupt nature; the eye does not see always; the Sea does not flow always; the Sun does not always shine: but the corrupt nature is always active. No sooner will the Spirit send up a good impulse, but the flesh will immediately try to repel it and extinguish it. The Devil does not always tempt, and the world does not always torment, but the flesh opposes the Spirit continually.

If it be so, that our corrupt nature possesses all these qualities, then humble yourself in the awareness of your corrupt nature: notwithstanding that you may be endowed with many noble gifts and graces, yet remain humble because, although you have a Divine nature <note>The "Divine nature" refers to the "new man" or the spiritual life implanted by grace, which exists alongside the old corrupt nature in a believer.</note> which always opposes it. It is just as it is with a peacock: though it has the finest feathers of all the birds on earth, it nevertheless has dirty feet; and like the swan, although it has the whitest feathers <note>The author uses traditional animal emblems: the peacock's "ugly" feet were often used to remind the proud to look down at their own failings, and the swan's black skin beneath its white feathers represented hidden corruption.</note>. For the flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary to one another; so that you do not do the things that you would.

<margin>1st Reason.</margin>
Firstly, the <term>corruption of nature</term> <note>This refers to "Total Depravity," the belief that every part of human nature is affected by sin.</note> remains, even in born-again people, in order to humble them; just as 
<margin>Deuteronomy 8:15, 16.</margin>
it was with the Israelites in the wilderness when they were bitten by fiery serpents and scorpions; it was to humble them. <note>The author refers to the biblical account in the Book of Numbers and Deuteronomy where God sent serpents as a discipline to teach the Israelites humility and reliance on Him.</note> So too, while we are in this wilderness of this world, we always have a corrupt nature clinging to us, by which we are stung; and these fiery serpents of sin must humble us before the Lord. God has so ordered it in nature that the most noble creatures have some visible ugliness, whether we look at the birds or at the four-footed animals. Among the birds, the peacock has the finest feathers, but it has the ugliest feet; the swan has the whitest feathers, but it also has the blackest skin; the eagle has the sharpest sight and flies the highest, but it is the most gluttonous among birds. The lion is the most magnificent and beautiful among the beasts, yet is the most fierce and cruel. # and SPIRIT.

<margin>The fifth question.</margin>
The fifth question is this: what rules must one follow so that the movements of the **flesh** toward **sin** do not gain the upper hand over the **Spirit**?

<margin>First rule.</margin>
First: if you do not want the flesh to overcome you in its sinful movements, then resist them while they are still merely impulses, before they break out into actions. Crush the **Basilisk** <note>A mythical serpent-like creature said to kill with its gaze; here used as a metaphor for a deadly sin that must be destroyed before it "hatches."</note> in the egg; trample on sin—which is the fire of Hell—while it is still a spark, namely in its initial suggestion and movement. Just as we say it is easier to keep an enemy out than to cast him out once he has been let in; so it is also easier to keep sin out than to cast it out. Sin in its initial movement is like an enemy in the suburbs who has not yet been let into the City: and if you do not wish to give in to these movements, then resist them while they are still in that state; extinguish them while they are only impulses.

<margin>Resist the beginnings; the medicine is prepared too late when the illness has grown strong through long delays. <note>original Latin: "Principiis obsta, sero Medicina paratur; cū mala per longas invaluēre moras." A famous maxim from the Roman poet Ovid.</note></margin>
If one pays attention to a disease in time, before the bad <term>humors</term> <note>original: "humeuren"; referring to the historical medical theory that the body was controlled by four fluids. If these became "imbalanced" or "gathered," it resulted in illness.</note> have gathered together, one can easily cure it. Now I proceed to the last question, which is this: How can one distinguish when the impulses toward sin proceed from the flesh, or when they proceed solely from the Devil, and are thus entirely diabolical? <margin>3rd Sign.</margin>
Thirdly, the temptations of Satan are commonly accompanied by much terror and fear when they are suggested. When a temptation attacks someone so strongly that it makes them tremble, and a terror comes over them, it is proof that it comes from the Devil; and the reason is this: because nature only incites one to those sins which are most pleasant to nature. Nature causes no "fire" <note>original: "brant"; in this context, it refers to a sudden, violent inflammation of the mind or a searing agitation of the soul that feels foreign to one’s own disposition.</note> in the mind.

<margin>4th Sign.</margin>
Fourthly, Satan’s temptations usually arrive when a suitable object and opportunity to commit a sin is present. Just as when someone, being troubled in his mind, sees the water, the Devil then tempts him to drown himself; or when he sees a knife lying there, he tempts him to take his own life; or when someone sees an object of beauty <note>original: "schoonheit"</note> before them and is then tempted toward unchastity—see, such temptations usually come from the Devil. It is true, the Devil can indeed disturb the imagination even when no object is present, but that happens seldom. We also have examples in the Scripture of those who, when the opportunities for sin appeared, were tempted by them.

<margin>Genesis 3 verse 6.</margin>

5. The Spirit of God suppresses the movements of sin: He not only resists them but also helps the person to put the movements of sin to death.

Thus you see how the Spirit sets Himself against the flesh in respect to sin.

<margin>II.</margin> 2. Just as the natural conscience does not extend itself to the sin of nature <note>original: *zonde der natuure*; referring to original sin or the inherent depravity of human nature</note>, so it does not extend itself to the nature of sin. This is my meaning: the natural conscience never battles against the nature of sin, but only against the punishment of sin. It does not rebuke a person for sin based on the observation that it is against a holy God and a holy and pure Law. Rather, the natural conscience only struggles against the punishment of sin, and not against the nature of sin itself. It is not because sin stains the soul, but because sin destroys the soul; not because sin erases the image of God, but because sin ensures that people shall not see the face of God; not because God hates sin, but because God punishes sin. 

But the reborn <term>reborn: Dutch *weder-geboorne*, referring to those who have experienced spiritual regeneration</term> do not only struggle through the Spirit against the sin of their nature, but also against the nature of their sin; against their sin, not as something destroying their souls, but as something infecting their souls; not as something tormenting the conscience, but as something staining the conscience; not as something damning the soul, but as something defiling the heart. A natural man <note>An "unregenerate" person who has not been changed by divine grace</note> may be terrified of sin, just as a child is afraid of a burning stick—not that he fears to handle it because it will make his hands black <note>i.e., dirty or soot-stained</note>, but because it would burn his fingers. <margin>The fifth distinction.</margin>
The fifth distinction is this: the struggle between Spirit and flesh and the struggle between the natural Conscience and sin are distinguished by their outcome; and in this, there is a fourfold distinction.

<margin>I.</margin>
First, this is the outcome of the struggle of a natural Conscience against sin: it leaves the person restless and the sin unslain <note>The Dutch *ongedoodet* refers to the theological concept of "mortification," where sin is not merely suppressed but "put to death" or deprived of its power.</note>. Such was the case with **Judas**; his Conscience told him—<margin>Matthew 27, verse 5.</margin>—that he had sinned by betraying his Master, and he was so distraught by this that he went away and strangled himself; yet, nevertheless, his sin remained unslain. But conversely, it is different with the struggle of the Spirit, which not only sets the mind at peace but also slays the sin. This is why the Apostle, having spoken of the struggle of the Spirit against the flesh, says that the <margin>Galatians 5, verse 22.</margin> fruit of the Spirit is joy and peace; this is the outcome of the struggle of the Spirit. It not only sets the mind at rest, but <margin>Romans 8, verse 13.</margin> also slays the sin: *If you through the Spirit put to death the deeds of the body, you shall live.*

the broth <note>original: *sop*; the author is likely referring to the liquid in which forbidden meat was cooked</note> might be a temptation for them to also eat the flesh: therefore, see to it that you give no opportunity <note>An "occasion" or opening for temptation</note> to the flesh against the spirit, so that you are not ensnared by it.

<margin>Augustine, *Confessions*, Book 6, Chapter 8.</margin>
*Augustine* relates an example here. A certain *Alypius* <note>A close friend of Saint Augustine; this famous story describes his struggle with an "addiction" to the violence of the arena</note> was drawn by the incessant and difficult persistence of his friends to be present at the *Gladiatorial Games* of the Romans: but being there, he resolved to keep his eyes closed the entire time, so that he, though present in body, would be absent in heart; but when a great shout occurred at the fall of one of the fighters, he opened his eyes, and thus became a spectator <note>original: *goet-kender*, literally a "connoisseur" or "keen observer"</note> of that bloody and barbaric spectacle; therefore, guard yourself against entering into the occasions of sin.

<margin>3. Rule.</margin>
Thirdly, if you do not wish for the flesh to rule over the Spirit, do not keep your thoughts and contemplations occupied with sin; to frequently imagine and behold sin weakens the movements and workings of the Spirit, and it strengthens the movements of sin in your heart. Of this speaks the Prophet *Ezekiel* in his 23rd Chapter, verse 19: *They multiplied their harlotries, remembering the days of their youth*: bodily impurity is caused by beholding the sin in the mind <note>original: *herssenen*, literally "the brains"</note>; and it is the way to strengthen the heart against the movements of the Spirit.

### Galat. 5. v. 17.

> For the flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; and these are contrary to one another, so that you do not do the things that you would.

<margin>
28th Sermon at St. Lawrence Jewry, <note>The Dutch "Lawrence Jurii" refers to the church of St Lawrence Jewry in the City of London, where many influential Puritan sermons were delivered.</note> in London, the 5th of January 1651.
</margin>

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial 'N' containing a floral and vine motif.</image-desc>
Now I proceed to the cause of this struggle / from whence it comes / that the flesh lusts against the Spirit / and the Spirit against the flesh; the Apostle gives here this reason; that these stand against one another. The words do not require much explanation: Only / regarding the statement of the Apostle / when he says that the flesh and the Spirit are in the same person / and that these two stand against each other / I establish this conclusion; that contrary things can be found in the same subject.

<margin>
Opposites cannot exist in the same subject in an intense degree. <note>original Latin: *Contraria nō possunt esse in eodem subjecto in gradu intēso.*</note>
</margin>
It is true / contrary things cannot be in the same subject in a strained and highest degree / but indeed in a lesser and lower degree; and so it is here. The Apostle speaks of the flesh and the Spirit in the same <term>regenerate person<gloss>A "born again" Christian who has received a new spiritual nature but still retains their old sinful nature, known as "the flesh."</gloss></term> / and of their contrariety against each other / not in the highest but in a lower degree. In the highest degree they cannot be there / because in Heaven there is perfect grace without sin / and in Hell there is nothing but sin / and no grace / but on earth

<meta>This page continues the sermon on Galatians 5:17, further exploring the theological concept of "contrariety" within the believer. It follows the argument from the previous page that two opposing forces can inhabit the same person if neither is at its absolute maximum intensity.</meta>

<page-num>283</page-num>
<header>and S P I R I T.</header>

Therefore we are partly sinful / and partly graced / and therefore these two opposites can very well exist together in a lesser degree in a <term>reborn person<gloss>In this context, a "reborn" or "regenerate" person is a Christian who has undergone a spiritual transformation but still struggles with their original sinful nature.</gloss></term>. These two stand against each other; it is impossible / to think of a more bitter opposition and a more direct contrariety of anything in the world / than between the flesh and the Spirit; there is no greater opposition between light and darkness / Heaven and Hell / fire and water / than between flesh and Spirit. Direct contrariety is more than enmity / for enemies can be reconciled / but direct contrariety never: certainly one direct opposite may cast out the other / but it cannot be reconciled with the other: water may extinguish fire / but it cannot be united with it; and light may drive out the darkness / but they can have no fellowship with each other. The direct contrariety of the flesh against the Spirit consists in this / that all the good / which the Spirit wills / the flesh does not will / and toward whatever evil the flesh incites / from that the Spirit warns: this is the direct contrariety / and the cause of the struggle in the reborn.

<margin>Doctrine.</margin>
The *Doctrine* is this: That there is a two-sided and irreconcilable direct contrariety between the *flesh* and the *Spirit*, between *nature* and *gifts of grace* in the hearts of *reborn* men.

I call it a two-sided or mutual <note>The author uses the term "twezijdighe" (two-sided) to emphasize that the conflict is not passive; both the sinful nature and the spiritual nature are actively attacking one another.</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 283 regarding the "mutual contrariety" (direct opposition) between the flesh and the Spirit. The previous page ended mid-sentence, defining why this opposition is two-sided.</meta>

<page-num>284</page-num>
<header>Struggle between flesh</header>

mutual direct contrariety, because it is not a one-sided opposition; rather, the flesh stands against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh. Furthermore, I call it an irreconcilable direct contrariety because, although enemies may be reconciled, direct opposites can never agree.

In treating this chapter, I will only prove the truth of this [opposition], and then I will conclude with an application to the practice of <term>godliness<gloss>In this era, "godliness" (Godtzaligheit) referred to the active, lived experience of Christian devotion and moral conduct.</gloss></term>.

<margin>1. Proof.</margin> And first, this direct contrariety appears from the conflicting names which are given in the <term>Scripture<gloss>The author refers to the Bible using the traditional term "Schriftuur."</gloss></term> to the flesh and to the Spirit; thus here in the text, corruption is called "flesh," and grace is called "Spirit"; corruption is called "darkness," and grace "light." *Romans 13 verse 12.* It is called a Law of death, but grace is called the Law of the Spirit of life, *Romans 8 verse 2.* Corruption is called the defilement of the flesh, *2 Corinthians 7 verse 1,* but grace is the purity of the Spirit, *1 Timothy 4 verse 12.* So that by these conflicting names given to the flesh and the Spirit, the direct contrariety of both is made known.

<margin>2. Proof.</margin> Secondly, they are conflicting in their cause and origin; for first, corruption is called the work of the Devil; and "for this purpose the Son of God was revealed, that he might destroy the works of the Devil." *1 John 3 verse 8.* But grace is called the work of God, *Philippians 1 verse 6.*

Secondly, <term>corruption<gloss>The Dutch "verdorventheit" refers to the innate sinful nature or "flesh" of a person.</gloss></term> is called the desire of the Devil, *John 8 verse 44.* But grace is called the fruit of the Spirit, *Galatians 5 verse 22,* so that they have a directly opposing origin. <margin>John 3 verse 6.</margin> That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit.

<margin>3rd Proof.</margin> Thirdly, they have directly opposing operations: the flesh is said to desire against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh. For this reason, sinning is called in the <term>Scripture<gloss>Referring to the Bible.</gloss></term>—<margin>Leviticus 26 verse 21.</margin>—walking in opposition to God. Sin causes a person to go against God, but the Spirit draws a person to walk in God's ways. Sin is like that <term>Delilah<gloss>A reference to the biblical figure who weakened Samson; the author uses her as a metaphor for how sin persistently pressures and seduces the believer.</gloss></term>, who never leaves a person alone, but pressures and troubles them to give in to the temptations of sin.

<margin>4th Proof.</margin> Fourthly, they are different in their end and outcome; the aim of the flesh is to bring the soul to damnation, but the movements and operations of the Spirit are meant to preserve the soul. We are commanded to abstain from fleshly lusts, which wage war against the soul; <margin>Romans 8 verse 13.</margin> the Apostle tells us that if we live according to the flesh, then we shall die: but if we through the Spirit put to death the deeds of the body, then we shall live. Sin leads toward death, but grace toward eternal life. And therefore the same Apostle says: <margin>Romans 8 verse 2.</margin> The Law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has made me free from the Law of sin and of death.

<margin>Third motive.</margin>
Thirdly, so that you might humble yourself, observe that this resistance of nature against grace works tirelessly within you: if this resistance only showed itself now and then on some unusual occasion, it would not be so significant; but this <term>corruption<gloss>Dutch: "verdorvent-heidt" — the theological concept that human nature is fundamentally tainted by sin.</gloss></term> works against grace without ever becoming weary. The gifts of grace and good impulses are supernatural, and therefore they are sometimes difficult and troublesome to us, who are flesh and blood; but the corrupt impulses toward sin are natural to man. Now, those things which work out of nature also work tirelessly: just as the sea is never weary of flowing, nor the sun of running its course, and just as the fire is never weary of burning, so also the corrupt nature is never weary of fighting the Holy Spirit. Our entire course and way to Heaven is "up the mountain," and against the tide and the wind of corruptions and temptations.

<margin>Fourth motive.</margin>
Fourthly, humble yourself on this ground: that this contradiction of nature against grace shall be constant, even until your dying day. It would be something if this resistance only came at times, and then nature grew weary, or if it stopped at a certain age of a person's life; but this corruption will oppose the gifts of grace as long as you live. # THE STRUGGLE BETWEEN FLESH

[commanded] you to do to your nature just as the Jews were required to do to their houses; they had to scrape all the stones <note>The author concludes the reference to Leviticus 14:41, where the walls of a house infected with "leprosy" or mildew had to be scraped to remove the contamination.</note>. Although our **gifts of grace** in this life will never be so strong that they could entirely expel our corruption, you shall nonetheless, by maintaining this struggle with all your power, so subdue your corruption that it will never extinguish grace.

<margin>Third reason.</margin>
Thirdly, you must know that not to struggle with your corrupt nature is a proof that there is no grace in you. There is no conflict within a single thing, but there must always be two. These stand against one another: just as the corrupt nature stands against grace, so grace also stands against the corrupt nature. Therefore, if you are at rest and quiet, and do not fight against your corruption, it is an evident proof that there is no grace in you.

Now I shall proceed to the two-fold result of this two-fold struggle, in which there is also a two-fold relationship: *The flesh desires against the Spirit*, so that you do not do the good which you would; and *the Spirit desires against the flesh*, so that you do not do the evil which you would. <margin>Doctrine.</margin> That the corruption of the flesh, even in the regenerate <note term="regenerate">Those who have been "born again" or spiritually renewed through faith, yet who still struggle with their old sinful nature.</note>, often turns them away from and disturbs them in their holy duties.

To confirm this, you have not only the testimony of the **Apostle** <note>Referring to the Apostle Paul.</note> that it stood thus with other men, but also his own experience; for thus he complains of himself: to will is present with me, but how to perform that which is good I find not.
<margin>Romans 7:18, 21.</margin> When I would do good, I find that evil is present with me.

I shall divide this **Doctrine** into two parts and show that this corruption of nature has a twofold evil consequence or effect in regards to that which is good.

First, it prevents a person from doing good. Secondly, it hinders a person while doing good.

**I shall now dwell upon these particular things and shall begin with the first:** That the corrupt nature prevents a person from doing good.

<margin>The first deceit of the flesh.</margin>
**First**, the flesh prevents a person from doing good by making him believe that he is *above* the use of religious duties: this suggestion arises from a proud and fantastical nature. Duties (say the foolish **Familists** <note term="Familists">Members of "The Family of Love," a 16th-century mystical sect that believed highly spiritual people were beyond the need for outward religious practices like the sacraments or formal prayer.</note>) are merely "fleshly forms" intended only for the lowest order of Christians, but not for those who have grown to a high stature and possess higher gifts. <meta>This page continues the discussion of the "eleventh trickery" of the flesh, which argues that because one has not committed "gross" or public sins, they need not be so diligent in their religious life. The author begins a five-point rebuttal to this spiritual complacency.</meta>

# AND SPIRIT #
<page-num>337</page-num>

This is a deceptive trickery of the corruption of the human heart; and therefore I shall say a little more about this: <margin>Remedies against this</margin> there are five things that I shall answer here.

<margin>I.</margin> Firstly, this argument smacks of pride, of laziness, and of ignorance: of pride, as if being very religious <note>original: 'Godtsdienstigh', meaning one who is diligent in the service and worship of God</note> could satisfy for sin; it smacks of laziness because the heart seizes upon such poor excuses to hold you back, or at least to cause you to neglect your religious duties; and then it also smacks of great ignorance, as if someone who commits many sins could be truly religious. No, the more you sin, the less you are able to serve God; and if your religious practices do not cause your sins to decrease, then your sins will cause your religious practices to decrease.

<margin>II.</margin> Secondly, observe that the Angels and the Saints in heaven have committed no sin at all; nevertheless, they continually serve God the Lord; they always sing songs of praise and Hallelujahs to God, yet never sin; and it is required of us to do God's will as it is done in heaven, that is, steadfastly and cheerfully.

It says there: *The Lord met him at the inn and sought to kill him*; what was the cause? See, it was only because he had neglected to circumcise his son when he was eight days old; this provoked God so much to anger that He sought to kill Moses. Yet Moses could have brought forward seemingly more plausible excuses for his neglect than we can for many religious duties that we neglect. I say this to show you the danger of the sin of omission.

<margin>V.</margin> Fifthly and finally, consider that you would not accept such an argument as valid in other matters. If your servants dealt with you in this way—that when you commanded them to do one work or another, or to perform such a service, and you demanded an account from them—would you then accept such an excuse if they said that they do not steal your goods from your shops, nor your money from your offices <note>original: "kantoren"—referring to the counting-houses or business rooms of Dutch merchants</note>; and that they do you no wrong? Would you accept those excuses? Certainly not.

...into the proposition which I intend to treat, I shall set forth these ten conclusions or <term>propositions</term> <note>original: "stellinghen"—foundational points or theses used in a logical argument or sermon.</note> concerning the flesh's hindrances in the good duties of the godly.

<margin>The first Proposition.</margin>
The first is this: that the corruption of the flesh is more powerful in disturbing the godly during holy duties than in leading them away from them entirely. Certainly, corrupt nature overcomes the unregenerate <note>Those who have not experienced spiritual rebirth or conversion.</note> in drawing them away from the service of God, but the opposite is true for the <term>born-again</term> <note>original: "wedergeboorne"—referring to those who have undergone a spiritual transformation.</note>. The godly are not so much subject to being drawn away from holy duties as they are to disturbances within them. The neglect of duties can be recognized as evil even by the <term>natural conscience</term> <note>original: "natuurlijke Conscientie"—the innate moral sense shared by all humans, even those without specific religious instruction.</note>, and therefore the godly are not so often overcome in that way; but concerning the hindrances *within* the duties, the natural conscience does not possess such knowledge.

<margin>The second Proposition.</margin>
The second is that a God-fearing person is more disturbed in his worship by his own heart than by the Devil or the world, or anything else outside of himself. We often accuse our occupation or the Devil—claiming that he goes about us so much and is busy ensnaring us—when we have more reason to blame our own evil hearts. Just as it is characteristic of the godly, when they sin, to accuse their own corrupt nature and not the Devil, as David did <margin>2 Samuel 24:10</margin>; so it is also when the godly are in their God's
->service<-

<margin>Third objection.</margin>

This is an objection of the **Pelagians** <note>Followers of Pelagius (c. 354–418 AD), who taught that human beings have the free will to achieve moral perfection without divine grace. This was a major point of contention for the author's Reformed or Calvinist worldview.</note>. <margin>Answer.</margin>
To this I answer / that although the **Godless** are so lacking in strength / **God** nevertheless has great reason / to command such things.

<margin>I.</margin>
Firstly / to let them see / what kind of people they once were; for in the **state of innocence** <note>The theological state of humanity before the Fall of Adam and Eve.</note> they were fully capable of doing the **will of God**.

<margin>II. God commands, not what we can do, but what we ought to do. <note>original: *Deus jubet , non quod possumus sed quod debemus.*</note></margin>
Secondly / although **God** commands men / that which they cannot do / this is nonetheless useful to **humble** <note>original: *verootmoedigen*; a central concept in this tradition involving the crushing of human pride to make room for grace.</note> them, so that they might through this bewail their own powerlessness.

<margin>III.</margin>

# The Conflict between Flesh [and Spirit]

To apply this to yourself, I will present three urgent considerations to you.

1. **In your religious services** there are more workings of sin, which proceed from the flesh, than of virtue which comes from the Spirit; would you then dare to place your trust in them? They contain more sin than virtue, and more wandering thoughts than holy ones! You forget more of a **Sermon** <note>original: "Predikatie"</note> than you remember of it, and the sin of your nature suggests more distracting thoughts than the Spirit of God suggests holy thoughts; your virtues are like gold filings, but your sins are like heaps of dust: how then would you dare to rest upon your religious services, expecting life and salvation through them?

2. **Consider** that a single circumstance is enough to make your religious service evil; but many concurring circumstances cannot make the same good. Suppose that you pray: a single circumstance in your prayer can make it sinful. Even if the manner of praying is good, if you nonetheless do not have a good end <note>In this context, "end" refers to the goal or intention of the act.</note> in view; or if the end is indeed good, but the origin is evil, then it 
<margin>In moral matters, the circumstance matters more than the substance of the action. <note>original: "In moralibus plus circumstantia quã substantia actionis." This is a common maxim in Scholastic philosophy, suggesting that for an act to be truly "good," every detail—intent, timing, and method—must be correct.</note></margin>
is of no value. It is a rule in **Ethics** <term>Ethics: Translated from "Zeede-kunde," referring to the study of moral conduct and the nature of right and wrong.</term> that the circumstances must be weighed more than the works themselves; and so it is also in **Theology** <note>original: "Godtgeleertheidt"</note>. A single circumstance can make an act of worship deficient, but many concurring circumstances can—

# The struggle between flesh #

Firstly, the ungodly are pulled away by the flesh <note>original: "vleesch"; in this theological context, "flesh" refers to the sinful, fallen nature of humanity rather than just the physical body</note>, but they do not have the Spirit as the godly do to stand against corruption.

<margin>
1 John 3
verse 9
</margin>
Secondly, the ungodly have no renewed principles of grace in their hearts to withstand the corruptions of the flesh, as the godly do. The born-again <term>born-again: "weder-geboorne," referring to those who have undergone a spiritual rebirth through grace</term> cannot sin (namely, in the same manner as the ungodly) because the seed of grace remains in them.

Thirdly, the ungodly do not distinguish so clearly, nor do they weep so feelingly <note>original: "gevoelijken"; expressing deep emotional or spiritual sensitivity</note> over the distractions of the flesh, as the godly do.

Fourthly, the ungodly shall never be released from the evil workings of the flesh, neither in this world nor in the world to come. Sin shall hinder their worship <term>worship: "Godts-dienst," the formal performance of religious duties and service to God</term> in this life, and in the next, it shall cut them off from it entirely. But the godly, though tormented by the flesh here, shall nevertheless be freed from it at some point. And thus I have finished the first part of the twofold consequence.
