### THE SPIRIT.

For through restraining grace a person can obtain these benefits:
1. That he does not commit so many and such great sins.
2. That he does not deserve such great punishment.

# Christ’s Prayer,

## For the Support of the Saints,

### *John 17, verse 15.*

> I do not pray that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one.

This chapter encompasses within it the last and most solemn prayer (which we find recorded) that Christ ever offered in the world with and for his disciples; as he was about to depart from them, he wished to leave them a prayer, being the best <term>testament<note>In this context, a "testament" refers to a final will or legacy left by a person before their death.</note></term> that he could make for them.

This entire 17th chapter, from the beginning to the end, contains nothing else but Christ’s prayer to his Father. In this, four things are to be noted:
1. The time when he offered this prayer.
2. The posture of the body that he used.
3. The manner in which he prayed.
4. The matter for which he prayed.

The time when he offered this prayer is indicated in two ways.

<meta>This page continues the analysis of Christ’s "High Priestly Prayer" (John 17), moving from the third circumstance (the manner of his prayer) to the fourth circumstance: the specific subjects and purposes for which he interceded.</meta>

### Christ’s Prayer

All the rest of the Prayer was for his Disciples / that God would keep them in unity and truth / and glorify them and all other Believers with him in Heaven. Notice here, then, the wonderful affection of Jesus Christ toward his Church and people; when he was about to die / he prays more for the salvation of their souls / than for his own life. Oh! herein is the overflowing love of Jesus Christ made manifest / that even as he now expected to die a painful / despised, and cursed death / taking upon himself the wrath of God / deserved by our sins / he nevertheless wished then to remember his chosen servants / in whose place he stood / and for whose sins he died / and that with such an expansion of his heart in Prayer.

<margin>Fourth circumstance: the matter for which Christ prayed.</margin>
The fourth circumstance in this Prayer of Christ / is the matter for which he prayed; and that is presented in two ways / by way of exclusion / namely, who those were for whom he did not pray / *I do not pray for the World*, verse 9. This is a <term>proof-argument<note>original: "bewijs-reden"; a logical point used in theological debate.</note></term> against those / who plead for universal redemption <note>original: "al-gemeene verlossinghe"; the theological doctrine that Christ died for every individual person, which the author—likely a strict Calvinist—is arguing against.</note>. If Christ would not spend his breath to pray for them / then he certainly would not pour out his precious blood / to obtain Heaven for them. After that, it is stated in an affirmative manner / for whom he indeed did pray. *I pray for those, whom you have given me, for they are yours.* You chosen and reborn / for you I pray—

<meta>catchword: for I.</meta>

<summary>This page describes Christ’s deep love for his followers, noting that as he faced a painful death, he prioritized their salvation over his own life. It also outlines a theological argument that Christ's prayer and sacrifice were intended specifically for the "elect" rather than the entire world.</summary>

<margin>The fourth Doctrine.</margin>
Observe from this: That no one dies unless God takes him away. If our life were in our own hands, we would live too long; and if our life were in the hands of our enemies, we would not live a single day longer. But now our life is in God's hands, and therefore we cannot die unless God takes our life away. And this indicates that the refuge of a Christian is under Divine protection; a godless man cannot thrust you out of the world before your time; God must take you out of the world. It may be, that your enemies are envious of you, and that those who hate you wish a thousand deaths upon you; nonetheless, this can be your comfort: you cannot die until God takes you out of the world. According to the manner of speaking in the Scripture, those who die are said to be *gathered to their fathers* <note>original: "verzamelt te worden tot haare Vaders"; a common biblical expression for death found throughout the Old Testament.</note>; You shall live just so long as God deems it fitting to gather you to Himself, having made you fit for glory. # The Closest Examination

<margin>
Doctrine.
</margin>

The **Doctrine** is this: That the children of men must necessarily, with the greatest diligence and above all things in the world, investigate this—namely, what they must do to be **saved**. In the treatment of this proposition, I will first set forth some warnings; secondly, I will give you the reasons; and then I will apply it to us all.

<margin>
1. Warning: No one is saved by their doing.
</margin>

Three warnings are to be taken into account here. First: although it is most necessary for the children of men that they examine what they must do to be saved, one must nevertheless be warned that while we must examine what we must do, we must not delude ourselves into thinking that we shall be saved *through* the doing. # Of a Good Christian.

Furthermore, notice the distinction that exists between the answer which Paul and Silas give to these questions, and the answer which Peter gives to them in *Acts* 2:38 <note>original: "Handel. 2. v. 38"</note>. Peter said to them, repent, and let every one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins, and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. Paul and Silas give this as an answer: Believe, and you shall be saved. Peter gives this as an answer: Repent, and you shall be saved. God here makes something special known: that these different answers were given by the Holy Spirit to the very same question; both their answers are true. Peter says, Repent, and you shall be saved, to show that such faith which is not accompanied by repentance is not true faith, but is a presumptuous confidence <note>A "presumptuous confidence" refers to claiming the promises of God while continuing to live in sin without a change of heart.</note>.

<margin>
Faith and repentance must be joined together.
</margin>

Paul says, Believe, and you shall be saved, to point out to you that the repentance which is not accompanied by faith is only a legalistic sorrow <term>legalistic sorrow: a sorrow for sin driven purely by fear of punishment or the requirements of the Law, rather than a transformative love for God</term>: therefore one says, Believe, and the other says, Repent, to show that you must join these two together. If only this answer had been given, "Believe and you shall be saved," then people might have said: "This is a short way to Heaven; one only needs to believe." Peter says, Repent, and you shall be saved, to show that both must be put into practice by Christians, 

<meta>catchword: that</meta>

<summary>This page discusses the harmony between the biblical commands to 'believe' and 'repent,' arguing that they are inseparable components of the Christian life. The author explains that faith without repentance is hollow, while repentance without faith is merely a fear of punishment.</summary>
<keywords>Paul, Silas, Peter, Repentance, Faith, Acts 2:38, Salvation, Legalistic Sorrow, Presumption</keywords>

<margin>
Faith and conversion must be joined together.

Furthermore, note the difference that exists between the answer which *Paul* and *Silas* give to these questions and the answer which *Peter* gives to them in **Acts 2, verse 38.** <note>The original Dutch uses "Handel." as an abbreviation for Handelingen, the book of Acts.</note> *Peter said to them, **repent, and let every one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ, for the forgiveness of sins, and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.*** *Paul* and *Silas* give this as an answer: ***Believe, and you shall be saved***; whereas *Peter* gives this as an answer: ***Repent, and you shall be saved.*** God makes something specific known through this: that these various answers are given by the **Holy Spirit** to the same question. Both of their answers are true. *Peter* says, *Repent, and you shall be saved*, to show that such faith which is not accompanied by **conversion** <note>original: "bekeeringhe"; in this context, it implies a total turning of the heart toward God.</note> is nothing but a presumptuous confidence. *Paul* says, *Believe, and you shall be saved*, to point out to you that the **repentance** <note>original: "berouw"</note> which is not accompanied by faith is only a legalistic sorrow <note>original: "wettische droefheidt"; this refers to a sorrow for sin motivated only by fear of the law's punishment, rather than a spiritual love for God.</note>. Therefore, the one says *Believe*, and the other says *repent*, to show that you must join those two together. If only this answer had been given—*Believe and you shall be saved*—then people might have sat idly; thinking this is a short way to Heaven, and one only needs to believe. But *Peter* says, *Repent, and you shall be saved*, to show that both must be put into practice by **Christians**,

## Of a Good Christian ##

the Apostle gives as the answer to the **Jailer’s** <note>original: "Stok-waarders"</note> question: "Believe in the Lord *Jesus Christ*, establish your salvation upon *Christ*, lean upon his blood, his merits, and his righteousness." Thus, learn what a great benefit and privilege the children of men enjoy, that they live under the <term>Covenant of Grace: the theological doctrine that salvation is a free gift from God through faith</term>; for although they cannot be saved through their own works, they can nonetheless attain it through what *Jesus Christ* has done for them. You cannot be saved through all your doing, but certainly through believing, resting, and trusting in *Jesus Christ*, waiting for salvation through that which he suffered in your place and for your benefit. If we had been placed under a <term>Covenant of Works: the concept that humanity could only be saved by perfectly obeying all of God's laws</term>, then this would have been our rule: "Do this and you shall live"; but the **Covenant of Grace** says: "Believe and you shall live." The condition of the **Covenant of Works** is that we ourselves must demonstrate to God a precise and perfect righteousness; another’s righteousness would not be enough. Also, in this Covenant, a little would not be accepted for much, nor the will for the deed; rather, the judgment of <term>acquittal: or "vry-sprekinghe," the legal declaration of being free from guilt</term> would only be proclaimed to you if you were without any stain and perfectly righteous; but the Sentence of damnation would be pronounced if you were found unrighteous in even the slightest matter

I answer: if you lived under a **Covenant of Works** <note>A theological term for a relationship with God based on the condition of perfect personal obedience to His laws.</note>, you would never be able to be blessed; because you can never keep the heard Word to that precise measure which is required in the Covenant of Works; for it commands a person to keep the entire Law perfectly, and that in one’s own person. But know this to your comfort, that you are under a **Covenant of Grace** <note>In Reformed theology, this is the promise of God to be merciful to sinners and provide salvation through faith in Christ rather than through human merit.</note>, which requires not a perfect, but a sincere obedience to God’s Law, and which accepts the will for the deed. Oh, remember that you are not under the Covenant of Works but of Grace, which accepts Christ’s obedience and suffering for you (if you are a believer) as if it had happened from you in your own person.

->### A Description of True Blessedness ###<-

It is noteworthy what is written in *Hebrews 11* <note>Specifically Hebrews 11:17: "By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac..."</note>. Through faith, *Abraham*, when he was tested, offered up *Isaac*; and he who had received the promises offered up his only-begotten son. *Abraham* did not actually and truly perform the deed <note>In the biblical account in Genesis 22, an angel stops Abraham before he strikes his son; however, the author emphasizes that in God's eyes, the internal "yes" was equivalent to the act.</note>; but because he intended it in his heart, and the desire and purpose of his soul was to obey God's commandment, it was counted in the Scripture as having been done.

If you indeed wished you could pray better, hear God's will better, and put it into practice more than you do, then this is counted by God as if you had already done so.

3. Then you will never be cleansed and <term>sanctified</term> from sin. 47, 48. <note>Sanctification is the theological process of being made holy or purified from the inclination to sin.</note>

*Question: Why does God thus withhold His Spirit?*

Answer, the reasons are these:
1. Because in former times you did not listen to the movements of the Spirit. 49.
2. Because you present your evil passions as movements of the Spirit. 50. <note>The author warns against mistaking one's own emotional impulses or desires for divine guidance.</note>
3. Because you more easily follow the promptings of the evil spirit than of the good Spirit. <term>ibid.</term>
4. Because you have deliberated on how you might commit sin. 51, 52.
5. Because you have misused the movements of the Spirit for wicked lusts. 53.

### *The Fourth Sermon.*

*Question: To what extent can God's Spirit be withdrawn from a child of God before and after sin.*

Answer. Before the sin.
1. That it does not reveal to you that the thing to which you are tempted is sin. 54.
2. That you fall into sin through the turbulence of your desires. 55.
3. That you would rather take counsel with <term>flesh and blood</term> than with God's Spirit. <term>ibid.</term> <note>A biblical idiom referring to human nature, worldly wisdom, or one's own physical impulses as opposed to spiritual guidance.</note>
4. That you will fall into that sin which most conflicts with the virtue in which you are most outstanding. 56, 57. <note>The idea that a person's greatest strength is often where they are most vulnerable to a specific, contrasting downfall.</note>

After the sin.

## *The Nineteenth Sermon.*

*Question: why does God allow there to be such a conflict against the Spirit even in the reborn?* <note>The "reborn" or "regenerate" refers to those who have undergone a spiritual rebirth in the Christian faith.</note>
Answer.
1. God does it for a clearer display of His grace. 301.
2. So that they would value Jesus Christ more highly. In the same place <note>original: "ibid.," an abbreviation of the Latin *ibidem*.</note>.
3. So that they would humble themselves the more. 302.
4. So that their grace would be exercised thereby. 303.

*Question: why must a person fight against the corruption that he nevertheless cannot root out?*
Answer.
1. Because otherwise that corruption will break out into one's life with greater violence. 304.
2. Because you can nonetheless suppress and weaken it. 305.
3. Because if you did not fight, you would [fail to] demonstrate that grace is in you. 306.

*Rules concerning this conflict.*
1. Always keep a diligent eye over your heart. 307. 308,
2. You must never lose heart. 309, 310, 311.
3. You must humble yourself in the feeling of this conflict. 312.
4. Trace all your actual sins back to this natural corruption. 312, 313. <note>The author suggests viewing specific sinful acts as symptoms of an underlying "natural corruption" or original sin.</note>
5. Do not side with the flesh against the Spirit. 314, 315.

## The Twenty-fifth Sermon.

### V. Doctrine. <note>original: "Leere," the section of a sermon where the theological premise is established</note>

*That God’s Spirit often restrains and preserves the <term>reborn</term> <note>original: "weder-geboorne," those who have experienced spiritual regeneration or conversion</note> from sin.* <note>The OCR "zo" is likely a truncation of "zonde" (sin).</note>

*Question: how the Spirit restrains a reborn person [and preserves] the good.* <note>The Dutch "wederhout het goede" literally means "restrains the good," but in context with the following points, it refers to the Spirit's work in restraining the believer from evil while maintaining their good standing.</note>

->Answer.<-

1. By making him see the sin. 40.
2. By stirring the conscience. In the same place.
3. By pouring into him a principle of grace and holiness. 41.
4. By bringing to his remembrance specific passages of Scripture against sin. In the same place.
5. By giving to the heart a reverence and fear for the presence of God. 40.

*Question: in what does this work of the Spirit consist, in preserving man from sin?*

->Answer.<-

1. That he does not commit the sin in the spirit. 40.
2. That he does not sin at that time or place in which he would wish to. In the same place.
3. That he does not sin in the same manner as an <term>unregenerate</term> person <note>original: "onherboorene," one who has not been spiritually reborn</note>. 40.

### *The Twenty-sixth Sermon.*

*Question: What is the difference between the <term>restraining grace</term> of the Spirit and <term>renewing grace</term>?* <note>In Reformed theology, "restraining grace" (*inbindende genade*) prevents a person from acting on sinful impulses, while "renewing grace" (*vernieuwende genade*) actually changes the heart's desires.</note>
*Answer.* That can be recognized by these seven distinguishing marks.
1. The <term>restraining grace</term> of the Spirit in the godless breaks only the works <note>meaning the outward actions</note>, but does not change the will of man toward sin. 416, 417, 418.
2. It makes a person leave sin because of the severity of the Law. 419. <note>Referring to the fear of divine punishment rather than a love for God.</note>
3. It makes a person leave only gross <note>obvious or outward</note> sins. *In the same place.*
4. It restrains a person against his will from sin. 420.
5. It causes a more intense desire to sin to be provoked after that restraint. 421.
